result: Myosin V regulates rapid refilling of release sites at short inter-stimulus intervals (≤5 s) but does not affect the release process itself at longer timescales. Inhibition with MyoVin-1 or PBP markedly reduced release site reuse probability at 1000 ms intervals, with effects dissipating at intervals >5 s.
evaluation: Claims C1-C5 provide converging evidence from paired-pulse experiments (C1, Figure 1B), appropriate DMSO controls (C2), and time-dependent analysis (C3, Figure 1C) with statistical support (Table 1). The interpretation that myosin V regulates refilling rather than exocytosis (C4-C5) is logically consistent with the time-dependent effects observed.

result: Myosin V inhibition does not alter the number or structural organization of release sites but causes a small yet significant spatial shift in release event localization toward the AZ periphery. The number of clusters and AZ size remain unchanged, while the average distance from release events to AZ center increases.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8 are supported by multiple independent measurements including cluster counting (Figure 1D), ultrastructural EM analysis (Figure 1E), and spatial localization analysis (Figure 1F), all with statistical validation (Table 1). The interpretation in C9 about peripheral site engagement is a reasonable inference from the spatial data.

result: Myosin V inhibition reduces synaptic release magnitude during high-frequency stimulation in a frequency-dependent manner, with larger effects at higher frequencies and no effect at 0.1 Hz. Both MyoVin-1 and PBP reduced release evoked by 50 Hz trains to half of control levels and slowed release kinetics.
evaluation: Claims C11-C17 are well-supported by vGlut1-pHluorin imaging data (Figures 2A-C), appropriate DMSO controls (C12), and frequency-dependence analysis across a wide range (0.1-50 Hz). The frequency-dependent effects and normal release at low frequencies (C16-C17) provide strong evidence against direct effects on exocytosis machinery.

result: Myosin V regulates both temporal and spatial aspects of release site refilling without affecting endocytosis or AZ size. Inhibition exacerbates peripheral release site usage during high-frequency stimulation, but does not alter AZ dimensions, endocytosis kinetics, or cause surface accumulation of vesicle proteins.
evaluation: Claims C18-C26 are supported by comprehensive spatial analysis (Figures 2D-F), ultrastructural EM (Figure 2—supplement 1B), endocytosis measurements (Figure 2—supplement 1C-H), and sequential train analysis. Multiple independent lines of evidence converge to support the conclusion that myosin V primarily affects refilling rather than endocytosis or structural organization.

result: Myosin V inhibition causes an activity-dependent vesicle docking defect. During sustained KCl depolarization, vesicles are localized farther from the AZ and the docked/tethered vesicle ratio is markedly reduced, but these effects are not apparent under basal conditions without stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C27-C30 are supported by rigorous ultrastructural LaSEM analysis (Figure 3A,C,D) with appropriate controls (Figure 3—supplement 1A,B) and statistical validation (Table 1). The activity-dependence is clearly demonstrated by comparing KCl-treated vs. untreated conditions. The quantification method using distance distributions is appropriate and independent of total vesicle counts.

result: Recycling vesicles undergo continuous bidirectional shuttling between two pools with constant rates. Over 50% of settled vesicles disappear and reappear multiple times in the same bouton, with disappearance rate 2-3 fold higher than appearance rate, consistent with a two-pool model where Pool II is 2-3 times larger than Pool I.
evaluation: Claims C32-C38 are supported by single-vesicle tracking data (Figures 4A,B,D,E and 5B-E) with quantitative rate analysis (Table 1). The two-pool model (C37-C38) is a reasonable mechanistic interpretation of the observed rate differences. However, the claim that disappearance/reappearance represents the same vesicle (C36) relies on indirect evidence (low labeling density) rather than direct tracking.

result: Vesicle disappearance is primarily caused by motion out of focus rather than exocytosis or axonal transport. In ~97% of cases, integrated synapse intensity remains unchanged during disappearance, vesicles can be tracked beyond initial disappearance with relaxed criteria, and vesicles show acceleration before disappearance. Only <3% of disappearances involve vesicles leaving the synapse.
evaluation: Claims C39-C49 are supported by multiple complementary analyses: integrated intensity measurements (Figure 4C, Figure 4—supplement 1D), PSF analysis (Figure 4—supplement 1G,H), extended tracking with relaxed criteria (Figure 4—supplement 1E,F), and velocity/displacement analysis (Figure 6D). The convergence of multiple independent lines of evidence strongly supports the conclusion that disappearance reflects Z-axis motion rather than fusion or exit.

result: Vesicle disappearance rate is reduced 2-3 fold during high-frequency stimulation in a myosin V-dependent manner, with fast onset (<0.5 s) and slow decay. Myosin V inhibition eliminates the activity-dependent reduction in disappearance rate without affecting baseline rates or appearance rates.
evaluation: Claims C50-C55 are well-supported by quantitative tracking analysis (Figure 5B,C,D,E, Table 1) showing differential effects of myosin V inhibition on disappearance vs. appearance. The kinetics (C51-C52) are consistent with known calcium dynamics (supported by citation). The selective effect on disappearance but not appearance (C54-C55) is clearly demonstrated.

result: Monte Carlo modeling captures vesicle disappearance dynamics with a single constant baseline probability (8.5×10⁻² fraction/sec) and shows that activity-evoked reduction can be modeled as a 3-fold instantaneous decrease in disappearance probability, with myosin V inhibition returning the rate to baseline during stimulation.
evaluation: Claims C56-C60 are supported by computational modeling (Figure 5A,B, Table 1) that successfully recapitulates experimental observations. The model provides quantitative parameters that match experimental data. However, the model makes simplifying assumptions (e.g., constant probability, random exchange) that may not fully capture biological complexity.

result: The two vesicle pools are hypothesized to represent a smaller RRP-like membrane pool (Pool I) near calcium sources and a larger internal recycling pool (Pool II) farther from calcium sources, with a 2-3 fold size difference consistent with previously described functional pools.
evaluation: Claims C61-C63 are explicitly stated as hypotheses (C61-C62) and rely on indirect evidence from pool size ratios and comparison to literature (C63). While the hypothesis is reasonable and consistent with the data, direct spatial localization of the pools relative to the AZ and calcium channels is not provided. The authors acknowledge this limitation in the Discussion.

result: EGTA experiments demonstrate spatial organization of vesicle pools: disappearance (from Pool I) occurs near calcium sources and is EGTA-insensitive, while appearance (from Pool II) is farther from calcium sources and EGTA-sensitive. Modeling suggests 75±11% of initially observed vesicles start in Pool I, with 25±11% in Pool II.
evaluation: Claims C64-C70 are supported by EGTA experiments (Figure 5B-E, Table 1) showing differential effects on disappearance vs. appearance rates. The interpretation about spatial localization relative to calcium sources (C65, C67) is reasonable given EGTA's known properties. The quantitative estimates (C68) rely on modeling assumptions but are internally consistent with the data.

result: Myosin V functions as a tether rather than a motor: vesicle displacement and velocity increase before disappearance under all conditions, but these increases are not affected by myosin V inhibition. Angular displacement is also unchanged by myosin V inhibition, indicating myosin V regulates vesicle retention at the membrane through tethering rather than driving transport.
evaluation: Claims C72-C82 are supported by comprehensive analysis of vesicle motion parameters (Figures 6B-E, Table 1). The key finding that myosin V inhibition does not affect the increase in mobility before disappearance (C74, C76, C78) provides strong evidence against a motor function. The interpretation that myosin V acts as a tether (C80-C82) is a logical inference from these observations combined with earlier findings.

result: Three key findings summarize myosin V function: (i) it regulates release site refilling during repetitive stimulation but not exocytosis itself, (ii) recycling vesicles undergo bidirectional shuttling with activity-regulated undocking but not docking, and (iii) myosin V functions as an activity-dependent tether at the plasma membrane rather than a transport motor.
evaluation: Claims C83-C87 are summary statements that integrate findings from multiple experimental approaches throughout the manuscript. Each component is well-supported by the grouped results above. These represent the main conclusions of the study and are appropriately supported by converging evidence from release measurements, EM analysis, single-vesicle tracking, and motion analysis.

result: Prior work establishes that myosin Va is the only vesicle-associated myosin family member, interacts with SNARE machinery in a calcium-dependent manner, and has been implicated in exocytosis in various cell types, though its role in presynaptic processes remains controversial due to conflicting knockout studies.
evaluation: Claims C88-C93 accurately represent published literature as indicated by appropriate citations. These claims provide important context for the current study. The characterization of the field as controversial (C90) is supported by citations to conflicting studies. The citation to Desnos et al. 2007 (C93) about docking defects in neuroendocrine cells is consistent with the current findings.

result: Release sites exhibit a spatial gradient of reuse probability from center to periphery that is activity- and myosin V-dependent. This spatial organization may relate to differential modes of release (kiss-and-run vs. full fusion), with myosin V potentially regulating the balance between these modes.
evaluation: Claims C102-C103 are supported by spatial analysis data (Figures 1F, 2D-F). However, the connection to kiss-and-run vs. full fusion (C104-C106) is speculative. While C104 correctly cites published work on spatial distribution of fusion modes, the authors acknowledge they cannot distinguish these modes with current tools (C105). The prediction about myosin V's role (C106) is explicitly speculative.

result: The observed bidirectional vesicle shuttling contrasts with the widely held view of unidirectional vesicle flow during recycling. Similar vesicle undocking/docking dynamics have been reported in other synapse types (hippocampal, ribbon, calyx of Held), suggesting this may be a common feature across synapse classes.
evaluation: Claims C107-C114 appropriately contextualize the current findings within existing literature. The contrast with prevailing models (C107, C71) is clearly stated. The comparisons to other synapse types (C108-C111) are supported by appropriate citations and show reasonable quantitative agreement with current estimates. The speculation about mechanistic connections (C113) is appropriately qualified.

result: Myosin V may function both as a tether at release sites and as a transporting motor during earlier recycling stages. Prior work shows myosin V supports axonal vesicle transport and directed motion within boutons, while myosin II supports recycling indirectly through actin dynamics rather than direct transport.
evaluation: Claims about dual roles (C31, C101) are explicitly speculative. While prior work on myosin V in axonal transport (C99-C100) and myosin II function (C96-C98) is appropriately cited, the integration of these functions into a coherent model requires additional experimental validation. The speculation about molecular mechanisms (C94) is reasonable but untested.

result: A model where two vesicle pools are both at the AZ but at different distances from calcium channels is unlikely because calcium channels are highly mobile within the AZ plane, exploring areas comparable to the entire AZ dimensions.
evaluation: Claim C115 is supported by appropriate citations to published work on calcium channel mobility. This argument is used to support the interpretation that the two pools are separated along the Z-axis rather than within the AZ plane. The logic is sound given the cited channel mobility data.

result: Methods description: Hippocampal cultures from E16-17 rat pups were used with appropriate ethical approval. Experiments used established imaging approaches with 80 nm pixel size, 10 nm focal stability, and ~20 nm vesicle tracking precision. Myosin V inhibitors were applied acutely (5-10 min) to avoid developmental effects and cell death from extended exposure.
evaluation: Claims C116-C126 describe experimental methods with appropriate detail and citations to established protocols. The technical specifications (C120-C121, C124) are clearly stated. The rationale for acute inhibitor application (C125-C126) is explained. The low basal release probability (C123) justifies the single-vesicle labeling approach. These methodological details are appropriate and well-documented.
